Write Your Own.name: Write Your Own
Write Your Own.description:
**Your character. Your first scene.** Describe what is happening when the story begins, who is involved and the mood you want. A few sentences are enough: a first lesson, an awkward reunion, a market dispute, a quiet day at home, or a journey already under way.

Choose the matching starting location from the list so the opening and map agree. For a particular room within that place, name it in your prompt. The list offers public places in Glowhaven, the four academy entrances, Brookmeadow, Drakenspire's market and Asterveil's landing terrace. Opening abroad can reflect a local or visiting background; it does not issue future portal permissions.

Use existing characters when you want a familiar face. Their established identity, responsibilities and willingness still matter. Describe your intended situation; your actual character setup supplies starting possessions, skills and mechanical grants.

Examples: “I'm outside the Everlight Library with an overdue book and a perfectly reasonable excuse. Begin as I reach the desk.” “I'm in Brookmeadow, helping at the mill for the first time. Start with the problem nobody warned me about.”

In multiplayer, the host writes the shared opening.

Red pennants snap above the entrance while a broad stream of students climbs toward Phoenix Wing Academy. Returning students call to friends across the court; first-years keep glancing between the doors and the papers in their hands. Somewhere behind the practice wall, a whistle cuts through the clack of wooden blades. The breakfast stall by the steps is doing excellent business with people who insist they are not late.

The registrar's desk has been set just inside the Main Hall. A clerk checks the new student's name against the admitted list, passes over a folded timetable, and points to the waiting benches. Admission is settled. Today is about finding the right room.

Hinae Komori moves aside to make space, holding her own timetable flat with both hands.

“I checked the room number three times. I still nearly followed the second-years.”

A bell sounds. The conversations travel into the hall in little waves as the first-years are called together. Up ahead, Kōhei Sanada waits beside the lectern, perfectly still beneath the red academy crest. He lets the last scrape of a bench die away before he speaks.

“Good morning. From today, you are students of Phoenix Wing Academy. You will study Magic Theory, Magical Combat, and Potions and Alchemy. You will attend the lessons on your timetables. Being talented will not excuse being absent.”

A few shoulders straighten.

“You will also learn when to stop. A duel is not improved by an unnecessary injury. A useful spell is not improved by casting it where someone is eating. We expect effort, preparation, and the sense to ask when you do not understand.”

His gaze passes over the hall without lingering on anyone.

“Your first lesson is Magic Theory, in the Lecture Hall. Haruki Saitō is expecting you after this welcome. Follow the signs through the east doors. Good luck.”

Kōhei Sanada gathers his notes and returns toward the Faculty Offices. The formal silence breaks at once into voices, bags being lifted, and somebody discovering that a timetable can be upside down. Hinae Komori studies the arrow by the east doors, then gives it a small, satisfied nod.

Along the east corridor, a student board carries society notices, a few offers of paid afternoon help, and a small handbill pointing to the guild's public request board. None of it calls for a decision before class.

The Lecture Hall doors stand open. Haruki Saitō is setting a travel mug beside the board as first-years file through. The new student enters with the others, with the first lesson still ahead.

The cyan banners above Gryffin Tail's entrance barely move in the morning air. Everything below them is moving at once. Students with instrument cases weave around students with books; two returning classmates are arguing about a result neither has brought along. First-years gather near a desk in the Lecture Wing, where the registrar is steadily reducing a formidable stack of timetables.

The new student's name is already on the admitted list. A timetable changes hands, still faintly warm from the copying charm. Its morning blocks list the required rooms in order. Fumito Sakurai, wearing a welcome-duty ribbon over his second-year uniform, directs the newcomers toward the first-year welcome gathering with the concentration of someone determined not to provide three alternative routes.

“Straight ahead. The demonstrations can wait until this afternoon. That instruction is also for me.”

In the Lecture Wing’s welcome area, Nahlah Qamar turns her timetable to compare its headings with the schedule posted nearby, then carefully frees the end of her tail from beneath a bench. Around her, first-years gather for the headmaster’s address; the Lecture Hall waits farther along the wing.

Norio Shibata checks the wall clock and steps onto the low dais at the end of the welcome area.

“Good morning. Welcome to Gryffin Tail Academy. Your required subjects are Magic Theory, Magical Engineering, and Magical Arts. Please keep the timetable you have just received. The copy on the noticeboard is for reading, not taking.”

His delivery makes the final distinction sound thoroughly necessary.

“Lessons occupy the morning block. Restricted rooms remain restricted. If you find an error in a record, bring the record to the office. If you find an error in an experiment, tell the instructor before repeating it.”

He closes his folder.

“Kei Aoki will begin your first Magic Theory lesson in the Lecture Hall shortly. I will be in the Faculty Offices if an administrative matter needs correcting. I hope your first term goes well.”

The applause is brief but genuine. Norio Shibata heads toward the Faculty Offices, and the first-years begin moving toward their classroom.

On the way down the Lecture Wing, a crowded board mixes club fliers with small paid errands and a notice about the guild's public requests. A student pauses to read the pay on one slip, then hurries along to class.

Inside the Lecture Hall, Kei Aoki sets a textbook and wand on the desk and checks the first marked page. The new student enters among the other first-years. The board is still blank; the lesson has yet to begin.

Dragon Hoard's Arrival Gallery fills with yellow coats, gold-trimmed robes, luggage straps, and the smell of somebody's hastily purchased breakfast. Returning students pass the expedition exhibits without slowing. The new first-years slow down at nearly every case, until a member of staff waves them toward the timetable desk in the Exhibition Hall.

The new student's admission is already confirmed. The registrar finds the name, hands over a folded timetable, and points out the morning lesson block. On the next bench, Suzune Mikazuki is reading her own copy with the stern attention she usually reserves for judging whether something is tall enough to reach.

“The notices are at a sensible height this year,” she remarks. “A remarkable breakthrough.”

The first-years gather at the far end of the Exhibition Hall, where seats have been arranged for the welcome. Beyond the broad doorway, the gallery remains busy with older students heading to their own rooms. This is the start of the academic year for everyone, not a school waiting empty for one arrival.

Miyu Asahina stands at the front with a bright smile and one small stack of notes.

“Good morning, everyone. Welcome to Dragon Hoard Academy! You have your timetables, so you already know the most important thing: where somebody expects you to be.”

A little laughter travels through the benches.

“Magic Theory, Spellcraft, and Magical Creatures are your required subjects. Your lessons are in the morning. Please remember that wanting to investigate something is the beginning of a plan, rather than permission to open its case.”

She sets the notes down.

“You will learn how to ask useful questions, prepare for uncertain conditions, and bring discoveries home without losing the discovery or yourselves. First, though, you will learn the fundamentals. Noriaki Takatsuki is taking your Magic Theory lesson in the Lecture Hall shortly after we finish.”

Miyu Asahina looks across the first-year benches, pleased and quite serious beneath the warmth.

“Good luck. If your timetable is wrong, find me in the Faculty Offices. If you simply dislike the first bell, I sympathize. It is staying.”

Miyu Asahina gathers her notes and heads toward the Faculty Offices as the first-years rise and follow the signs to their classroom.

A board beside the Exhibition Hall exit holds notices for student societies, occasional paid assistance, and the guild's public request listings. The amounts vary; the first class is not waiting for anyone to browse them.

In the Lecture Hall, Noriaki Takatsuki squares a stack of paper against the desk. His spectacles catch the light as he studies the empty board. The new student steps inside with the arriving class, just before the first lesson begins.

Violet awnings shade the arrivals at Hydra Head, where the opening morning has filled the court with voices. Returning friends greet each other over traveling bags. First-years compare papers, look for signs, and try to judge which of the confident people ahead of them actually knows the way. From the garden comes the scent of flowers; from Confluence Hall comes a firm request to stop blocking the timetable desk.

The new student's admission is settled. At the desk, a clerk finds the name on the first-year list and hands over the schedule. The first lesson is marked clearly, with room numbers beside the remaining morning blocks.

A call goes up for the first-year welcome. The newcomers move into Confluence Hall, where benches have been arranged facing a small lectern. Through an open side door, an older group is already heading toward its own classroom. Somewhere behind them, a decorative ribbon makes a determined attempt to accompany the wrong coat.

Kiyoko Fujinami waits until the last arrivals have found space.

“Good morning. Welcome to Hydra Head Academy. You are now members of a school where many people share rooms, equipment, and the consequences of one another's decisions. We will try to make that a pleasant experience.”

Her pause leaves just enough room for a few uncertain smiles.

“Magic Theory, Enchantment, and Herbology are required subjects. Follow the morning lessons on your timetables. Keep track of announced practicals and examinations; a rumor that a practical has been cancelled is not an official notice.”

She rests one hand on the lectern.

“You do not need to know everything today. You do need to ask rather than quietly use something you cannot identify. Respect another person's work, return shared materials, and remember that a useful disagreement can be conducted at an ordinary speaking volume.”

Kiyoko Fujinami turns slightly toward the corridor.

“Your first Magic Theory lesson is with Kana Fujimoto in the Lecture Hall. The signs lead directly there. I will return to the Faculty Offices after this welcome. Good luck with your first morning.”

As she leaves, the room fills with movement. The first-years follow the timetable signs toward the Lecture Hall.

In the corridor, a noticeboard offers clubs, community errands, and occasional paid afternoon help; a little guild notice is tucked beneath the others. A few students glance at it before following the classroom signs.

Kana Fujimoto has arranged a few ordinary teaching examples beside the Lecture Hall board. She looks up as the first-years arrive, smiling with a trace of nerves. The new student enters the room. The lesson has not started.

The first-year welcome is over by the time the new instructor reaches Phoenix Wing's Faculty Offices. Outside, the morning's scattered voices are settling into the more regular sounds of lessons. Inside, Kōhei Sanada has cleared a space on his desk for an appointment letter, a teaching timetable, and a short list of rooms.

“Good morning. You must be our new instructor.”

He checks the name on the letter and indicates the chair opposite him.

“Your appointment is in Magical Combat. Ritsu Kurogane remains the course professor; you will be teaching the introductory group alongside the department. Your first supervised lesson is tomorrow, at the first bell, in the Training Yard.”

He taps that line once, then leaves the timetable where it can be read.

“Today, inspect the space and prepare a short opening exercise. Ritsu Kurogane can show you the boundaries and the practice equipment. Start with something your students can actually do. I would rather see them learn one useful thing than watch a demonstration they cannot follow.”

A sharp impact sounds outside, followed by an instructor's correction. Kōhei Sanada waits a moment, apparently satisfied by the second sound.

“Follow the teaching block on your timetable and keep your consultations and agreed duties. If a student is injured, stop the exercise. If you need different equipment, ask before the lesson.”

His gaze returns to the new instructor, direct rather than unfriendly.

“You have the rest of today to get ready. What would you like clarified before you see the yard?”

Norio Shibata has the new instructor's folder ready before the knock at his office door. The first lessons of the year are underway beyond the Lecture Wing; here in the Faculty Offices, a kettle hums beside a gray tray of completed forms.

“Come in. New instructor? Good morning.”

He compares the appointment letter with the folder, then turns the teaching timetable around.

“Magical Engineering. Sōichirō Takamine leads the subject. You are taking an introductory group in the Research Rooms at the first bell tomorrow. You are an additional instructor, not his replacement.”

The explanation is delivered without ceremony, as though preventing that particular misunderstanding has become part of the job.

“Today, find the room, check the available teaching apparatus, and decide on your first exercise. Sōichirō Takamine can answer questions about the course materials. Please arrange access to anything restricted instead of discovering that the cabinet is locked while a class waits.”

Norio Shibata draws a small pencil mark beside the room name.

“Morning lessons follow the timetable. If this room assignment is wrong for the equipment you need, tell me today. I can correct a timetable. I cannot make two classes fit through the same door.”

He sets the pencil down and opens his notebook to a clean line.

“Tomorrow, first bell. Research Rooms. Is there anything you need before you begin preparing?”

The door to Dragon Hoard's Faculty Offices is open, and Miyu Asahina is directing a procession of paper slips into three trays. She catches one before it joins the wrong stack, places it by hand, and looks up at the new instructor with a bright smile.

“Welcome! Yes, that's your appointment letter. Wonderful. You're the person I was expecting.”

She brings the teaching timetable onto a clear part of the desk.

“You're joining Magical Creatures. Genzō Iwakura leads the subject, and you'll be taking an introductory observation lesson tomorrow at the first bell, in the Discovery Labs. Start with the teaching specimens and records. Nothing needs to be released, chased, or brought back from a mountain today.”

The smile does not diminish when she says it.

“Today, go through the room with Genzō Iwakura, check what you can use, and prepare one manageable exercise. We want students to notice something accurately before they become wonderfully confident about noticing everything.”

She traces the morning block on the timetable. Each classroom and teaching duty has been marked neatly.

“Your normal teaching sits here. Preparation and consultations can fit around it, and we'll agree on any extra duties separately. You do not need to volunteer for an expedition to make a good first impression.”

A slip of paper drifts toward her elbow. She pins it under the empty tray without looking away.

“First bell tomorrow. Discovery Labs. One useful lesson. Does that give you what you need, or shall we sort something out before you meet the department?”

A quiet knock brings an answer from Hydra Head's Faculty Offices. Kiyoko Fujinami has set an appointment book beside a small tray of tea. Beyond the window, students cross the Garden Walk on their way to morning lessons; the office itself is calm enough to hear the cups settle.

“Good morning. Our new instructor, I presume. Please come in.”

She reads the appointment letter, checks one entry, and places the teaching timetable within easy reach.

“You are joining Enchantment. Reon Fujisaki leads the subject. Your first introductory session is tomorrow at the first bell, in the Seminar Room. He knows to expect you today.”

A small pause follows.

“He may call you darling. It is not an administrative title.”

Kiyoko Fujinami turns the timetable to show the morning block.

Morning sun falls in green and honey-colored pieces across the guildhall tiles. Someone at the request board is arguing that a delivery cannot possibly count as an expedition. The person beside him points at the distance written on the slip and keeps chewing her breakfast.

At the counter, a young woman in a brick-red waistcoat is drawing something with far too many legs in the corner of her own scrap paper. Her peach-colored ponytails shift as she looks up, blue eyes bright.

“Welcome. New registration, looking for work, or here to explain why the parcel is making that noise?”

Komugi Hanabishi slides the scrap beneath a ledger with a completely unconvincing air of innocence.

“If you’re applying, we’ll start with the licensure assessment. You can use what you actually know—blade, bow, magic, whatever your method is. If you already have a genuine badge, show me and we can look at the board.”

Behind her, marked drawers hold records. Across the hall, bronze, silver, gold and pale platinum tabs divide the notices. A kettle clicks softly near the communal tables; beyond a rear doorway, a practice target swings and settles.

The North Arcade is opening for business. Wooden shutters knock back into place, a cart wheel protests at the paving, and warm bread competes with lamp oil in the morning air. Near the arcade's edge, Rinpei Komatsu lifts a little brass bird from a folding display case.

It sings three beautiful notes.

Then it sneezes.

"That last part is intentional," Rinpei tells the newcomer. "The first prototype just stopped. Customers felt judged."

He sets it beside a row of household trinkets and smooths the persimmon sash at his waist. Behind him, his repair screwdriver lies on a square of cloth. A handwritten card separates working stock from demonstration pieces.

"First morning trading here? Best advice I can give you: ask what a space costs before someone starts helping you fill it. Very friendly market. Astonishingly enthusiastic about fees."

Beyond his stall, an empty patch beneath the awning offers shade, but no sign says who controls it. Porters are already unloading farther along the arcade. The fountain sounds through the gaps between shouted prices.

Rinpei studies the newcomer with open professional interest.

"Looking to sell, buy, find a supplier, or work out what people here will actually pay for? Those are four different conversations. Usually all before breakfast."

Grain dust floats through a shaft of sunlight in Brookmeadow's Mill Lane. Beyond the working yard, water turns with a steady wooden clatter. Cottages line the quieter side of the lane; farther off, the Village Green carries the voices of people setting out for the day's work.

Haruho Taneda stands over two sacks with a tally slate in one hand and a deeply dissatisfied expression.

"Well, one of these has been marked twice, or somebody's grown a very modest extra harvest."

He brushes dust from a clean patch on the nearer sack, compares the marks, and shakes his head. His patched apron is already flour-white at the waist. A breeze stirs the corner of a covering cloth, and he secures it with his elbow.

"Morning. If you've a moment, can you tell me whether that's a three or an eight? I've been staring at it long enough to dislike both."

There is nothing alarming about the sacks. A few need moving under shelter before the weather changes, and a cart by the gate has a wheel awaiting a repair. The road toward Glowhaven remains open beyond the town, but here the immediate business is grain, neighbors, and whether the roof over the yard will keep another season's rain out.

Haruho turns the slate so its smudged figure is easy to see.

"No hurry if you're going somewhere. It'll still be an irritating number when you get back."

Warm light strikes the red practice banners and a stubborn line of chalk refuses to stop glowing. On the far side of it, Hinae Komori kneels beside an open notebook, her short wand still raised. A seed packet lies overturned beside a careful drawing of what appears to be a very small leaf spirit.

The last thread of the summoning circle curls inward. Where there should have been a modest practice familiar, there is now a person.

Hinae Komori stares. She checks the drawing. She checks the circle.

“That is… quite a lot more person than I expected.”

A chair scrapes behind her. Haruki Saitō sets down his coffee and approaches without stepping over the remaining chalk.

“Wand down, Komori. Say hello first. We can be confused politely.”

She lowers the wand so quickly that it nearly catches her sleeve.

“Hello. I'm Hinae Komori. This was supposed to be a supervised familiar exercise. I really am sorry.”

A faint strand of light runs from her wrist toward the newcomer, then sinks from sight. The chalk brightens once more. Hinae Komori flinches as a hot fleck lands against her fingers; the newcomer feels a small answering ache beneath the ribs. Haruki Saitō brushes the fleck away with a cloth.

“Connection,” he says, studying the fading line. “Not permission to order somebody about. We should establish what happened before anybody repeats it.”

Beyond the yard wall, a class is arguing about whose turn it is to carry the practice shields. Somewhere a whistle blows. The academy is carrying on with its morning, apparently unaware that one familiar exercise has become a rather different conversation.

Hinae Komori leaves the space before the circle clear and sets her notebook down.

“Are you hurt? And… what should I call you?”

Cyan curtains stir beside a high window. A completed spell diagram occupies most of the seminar-room floor, its angles measured so carefully that the chalk beside the ruler has worn almost flat.

The circle gives a tired little chime. Someone inside it wakes to the smell of chalk, paper and singed ribbon.

Satoru Kanda stands at its edge holding three pages of notes in the wrong order. For a long moment he looks delighted that something has happened at all. Then he notices what has arrived.

“No. Wait. That is not the… the specified familiar.”

Kei Aoki looks up from the practical sheet. He looks at the circle, then at Satoru Kanda.

“Tch. I said a small supervised call.”

“I know. I can explain the entire structure. I just can't explain that part.”

He points helplessly at the newcomer, realizes what he has done and lowers his hand. His cheeks redden. The chalk at his feet gutters as the failed outer ring collapses. He takes a careful step back. A faint thread briefly catches the light between the newcomer and his empty hand, then disappears.

Kei Aoki extinguishes the remaining chalk with a small deliberate motion.

“Don't cast again. Both of you stay clear of the damaged edge.”

The inner connection remains as a faint pressure, then settles. Satoru Kanda puts his notes on a chair where nobody will have to stand on them.

“I'm Satoru Kanda. I was trying to demonstrate a beginner familiar exercise. This isn't a secret technique. I genuinely have no idea how I managed it.”

Outside, a bell starts the next part of the morning. Nobody in the room moves toward the door.

Kei Aoki folds the sheet once. “Ask their name before you start theorizing at them.”

Satoru Kanda swallows and looks back to the circle.

“Right. Hello. What should I call you?”

A gold-trimmed practice cloth covers the laboratory floor. There are little bowls of treats beside the summoning marks, a padded basket outside the circle and a wooden staff leaning against a cupboard where its owner has plainly forgotten it.

The circle opens like a bright ring on water. A person wakes in the middle of it.

Kōsuke Shishido is halfway through shaking a bag of treats when he notices.

“Oh! Hello.”

He looks at the basket, then at the person, and quietly pushes the basket behind his leg.

“I should probably have asked about size.”

From the next bench, Madoka Narukami brings her long wand down with a crack that silences the room.

“Shishido. That is a person. Stop offering them dried liver.”

He looks stricken at the bag in his hand. “These are the expensive ones.”

“Put. Them. Down.”

He obeys. A nervous little summoned animal peeks from beneath the bench, steals one escaped treat and disappears again. Kōsuke Shishido turns to find his staff, catches his knuckles against the cupboard latch and winces. At the same moment, a small ache answers beneath the newcomer's ribs. A fine golden thread glimmers between them and vanishes into ordinary light.

Madoka Narukami studies the fading circle, composed except for a very small movement beside one eye.

“Do not repeat the call. Do not give orders. And do not lose the staff while I am looking at it.”

Kōsuke Shishido finally retrieves it and puts it safely on the bench.

“I'm Kōsuke Shishido. I summon familiars. Usually quite a lot less conversational than this, but—well, you're welcome to talk.”

He pulls an empty chair closer to the circle without assuming anyone wants to sit. His grin returns, gentler this time.

“Would you like water? Or should we start with your name?”

Violet ribbons hang from the seminar-room windows, and somebody has arranged a summoning circle between two tables with admirable care. Beside it lies a handout entitled only by a neat block of unreadable classroom print. A cushion waits under the nearest chair.

The inner ring blooms with light. A person wakes inside it.

Tōma Utsugi, who had been prepared to greet something small enough to carry a stack of books, says nothing at all. His eyes travel from the newcomer to the handout.

“Oh.”

Reon Fujisaki turns from the window. The enchantments in his pink eyes catch the light as he takes in the scene.

“Darling, I do believe your shortcut has acquired an opinion.”

“It hasn't said anything yet.”

“Then be charming before it does.”

Tōma Utsugi straightens his crooked collar. For once the neatness is real rather than an illusion. A faint line hangs between the newcomer and his hand, glimmers once, and fades.

Reon Fujisaki's teasing expression softens into professional attention.

“There is a connection. We will examine it carefully. You haven't acquired ownership of anyone, Utsugi.”

“I was hoping for help carrying things.”

“Then perhaps you might ask.”

The corridor beyond is full of ordinary academy noise: shoes on stone, an argument about a missing spoon, somebody laughing far too loudly for a nearby study room. The failed expectation of a convenient little familiar hangs in the air beside a much more immediate question.

Tōma Utsugi puts the handout down and makes room at the edge of the circle.

“I'm Tōma Utsugi. I think we've both had a more complicated morning than planned. Are you all right?”
